chapter_title: Orienting Yourself: The Use of Coordinates
subject: mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 50 minutes × 6 periods = 300 minutes
Total: 6 periods · 5h 0min

periods.activity_title: Grids, Numbers, and Location: A Historical Entry Point
periods.visual_aids: Board sketch of a simple grid with a few labelled cells illustrating grid-based location

time_bands.activity: Open by posing the question: how would you describe the exact position of a point on a flat surface to someone who cannot see it? Students share ideas briefly in pairs. Collect a few responses on the board, noting what information every answer seems to need.

Walk through the chapter's account of grid-based thinking and coordinate geometry in Bharat, its transmission through Arabic mathematics, and Brahmagupta's formalisation of zero and negative numbers. Pause at each landmark to ask students why each development was necessary — why a grid without negative numbers is limited, what a formalised zero enables. Students note key ideas in their own words.

Students write a short response (three to five sentences) answering: 'Why did the four-quadrant coordinate plane require Brahmagupta's work on zero and negative numbers?' They then compare with a neighbour and refine their reasoning.

Whole-class share: two or three students read their responses. Consolidate on the board the chain — grid framework → negative numbers → four-quadrant plane — as the conceptual foundation the chapter builds on.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit grounds the chapter in the intellectual history that made a four-quadrant plane possible, so students enter the formal system with a sense of why it is structured the way it is. Watch for the common conflation of 'zero' with 'nothing' — stress that Brahmagupta's zero is a number occupying a position, not an absence. End of Chapter Q5 (p.12) is a good self-study read for a student who wants to extend this reasoning.

periods.activity_title: Mapping a Room: Grids Before Axes
periods.visual_aids: Board drawing of Reiaan's room outline on a rectangular grid at 1 cm = 1 ft scale, showing pins at corners

time_bands.activity: Introduce Reiaan and Shalini's project: representing a real room on a rectangular grid using pins and thread before any axes or coordinates are named. Ask students what information they would need to place a pin for, say, a doorway — scale, a reference point, distances. Record their answers as a checklist.

Students sketch Reiaan's room on their graph paper at 1 cm = 1 ft, marking corner pins. Working individually, they then mark the positions of the room door and bathroom door as pins on the grid, measuring from a chosen corner. The task is entirely at the informal grid level — no axis labels or coordinate notation yet.

Pair discussion: compare sketches. Where do the two partners' pin placements agree and where do they differ? What made it hard to communicate the position of a pin precisely without a shared reference? Students identify what is missing from the informal system and what a fixed common reference point would give them.

Whole-class consolidation: collect the 'what is missing' list. Guide students to articulate that a fixed origin and a direction convention are needed before the grid becomes a coordinate system. Leave the vocabulary 'axis' and 'origin' as a question the next part of the chapter will answer.

periods.teacher_notes: Having established the historical motivation for a grid-based location system in the earlier part of the chapter, this unit builds the informal precursor — Shalini's scaled room plan — that Section 1.3 will formalise. The most common difficulty here is students choosing different corners as their reference, producing incompatible pin positions; use this as a productive illustration of why a shared, named origin is essential. Students who finish early can try placing a piece of furniture (say a 3 ft × 2 ft bed) and describing its position to a partner using only distances from the chosen corner.

periods.activity_title: Axes, Quadrants, and Coordinates: Defining the Cartesian Plane
periods.visual_aids: Board diagram of the full Cartesian plane with labelled axes, origin, and the four quadrants showing sign patterns

textbook_items_in_class.description: Using Fig. 1.3 (Reiaan's room with corners O, A, B, C marked on the axes), find the distance of the door D1R1 from the y-axis and x-axis, state the coordinates of D1, find the door's width given R1 = (11.5, 0), and compare the bathroom door width (B1 (0,1.5) to B2 (0,4)) with the room door's width.

time_bands.activity: Formally define the x-axis and y-axis as two perpendicular number lines meeting at the origin O = (0, 0). Introduce the sign convention (right and up are positive, left and down are negative) and the four quadrants with their sign patterns: (+,+), (−,+), (−,−), (+,−). Draw the full plane on the board. Define the coordinates (x, y) of any point: x is its perpendicular distance from the y-axis (with sign), y its perpendicular distance from the x-axis (with sign). Students copy and label the diagram.

Think-and-reflect moment: pose the two questions from Section 1.3 — 'Must a point on an axis have a zero coordinate, and which one?' and 'Does swapping a point's coordinates ever give the same point?' Students write a one-sentence answer to each and discuss with a neighbour before the class settles on the answers together: a point on the x-axis has y = 0; swapping gives the same point only when x = y.

Students work through Exercise Set 1.1 (i)–(iv), p.5, applying the coordinate definitions to Reiaan's room plan: locating the door D1R1 from the axes, reading off D1's coordinates, computing door widths by coordinate difference, and comparing the bathroom door width with the room door width. Work individually, then check in pairs.

Discuss answers whole-class, focusing on the sign-convention steps and the meaning of a zero coordinate for points on the axes. Clarify any error in reading coordinates versus computing distances from axes.

periods.teacher_notes: The informal grid model of the room plan is now formalised: the corner Reiaan used as a reference becomes the origin O, and the walls become the positive halves of the axes. A persistent error at this stage is students reading the x-coordinate as the distance from the x-axis (rather than from the y-axis); reinforce by asking 'which axis do you move parallel to in order to reach the point?' as a mnemonic. Exercise Set 1.2 Q1–Q4 (p.8) is available for self-study for students who want additional room-plan practice.

periods.activity_title: Coordinates in Context: Room-Plan Problems and the Ordered Pair
periods.visual_aids: Board display of Fig. 1.3 room plan with axes and labelled points for reference during discussion

textbook_items_in_class.description: Given three feet of a rectangular study table at (8,9), (11,9), (11,7), find the fourth foot's coordinates, judge whether the spot is suitable, and state the table's width and length from the coordinates.
Sketch an 18 ft x 15 ft dining room running from point P to point A and mark its corner coordinates; place a 5x3 ft dining table at the centre of the room and give the coordinates of its feet.
Given point W with x-coordinate -5, predict the coordinates of point H on the line through W parallel to the y-axis, and state which quadrants H can lie in.

For a city grid of 10 streets in each of the N-S and E-W directions spaced 200 m apart, draw a 1 cm = 200 m model and, using the (N-S street, E-W street) intersection convention, find how many intersections can be labelled (4,3) and how many can be labelled (3,4).

time_bands.activity: Brief recap by posing a quick oral question: 'A point has coordinates (−3, 0). Which axis does it lie on, and which quadrant(s) is it NOT in?' Take two responses, then move immediately into problem work.

Students work through Exercise Set 1.2 Q1 (p.8) and Exercise Set 1.2 Q4 (p.8) individually on graph paper: finding the fourth table leg from three known coordinates, reading off dimensions from the ordered pairs, sketching the dining room and locating a centred table's feet. Teacher circulates and probes reasoning — 'how did you decide where the fourth vertex must be?'

Students attempt End of Chapter Q2 (p.12) and End of Chapter Q14 (p.13) — predicting which quadrants a point with a fixed negative x-coordinate can occupy, and drawing the city street grid to reason about why (4,3) and (3,4) label different intersections. Pair discussion on Q14 before whole-class check.

Consolidation: on the board, confirm that ordered pairs are directional — (4,3) ≠ (3,4) unless the two values happen to be equal — tying back to the think-and-reflect from the defining unit. Collect common errors seen during circulation and address them explicitly.

periods.teacher_notes: Building on the definitions established for the Cartesian plane, this unit gives students extended practice applying the ordered-pair convention in varied spatial contexts. Watch for students who treat x and y symmetrically and swap coordinates freely — End of Chapter Q14 is particularly useful for exposing this error because it makes the asymmetry of (4,3) vs (3,4) vivid in a real-world grid. End of Chapter Q3 (p.12) is suitable self-study for a student who wants to predict and verify axis-parallel and perpendicular sides from coordinates alone.
homework: Exercise Set 1.2 Q2 and Q3, p.8 — determine whether the bathroom door hits the wardrobe and identify bathroom-corner coordinates and the showering area shape.

periods.activity_title: Deriving the Distance Formula from the Baudhayana-Pythagoras Theorem
periods.visual_aids: Board diagram of a right triangle ADM in the first quadrant with points (x1,y1) and (x2,y2) labelled, showing horizontal leg AD, vertical leg DM, and hypotenuse AM

textbook_items_in_class.description: Plot point Z(5,-6), construct a right-angled triangle IZN, and find the lengths of its three sides.

time_bands.activity: Open with the question: given two points on the coordinate plane, how would you find the straight-line distance between them without measuring? Students suggest ideas. Establish on the board that a point on the x-axis or on a line parallel to it has its distance to a neighbour on that same line found simply by subtracting x-coordinates (or y-coordinates for a vertical line) — work one quick numerical example each.

Derive the general distance formula. Draw two points A(x1, y1) and M(x2, y2) in the first quadrant on the board. Construct the right triangle by dropping a vertical from M to meet the horizontal through A at D. Identify AD = |x2 − x1| and DM = |y2 − y1| as the legs. Apply the Baudhayana-Pythagoras theorem to get AM = √((x2−x1)² + (y2−y1)²). Pause to note why squaring removes the need for absolute-value signs. Then redraw the same triangle with the points shifted into negative-coordinate regions and confirm that the formula is unchanged — the squares absorb the signs. Students record each step.

Think-and-reflect: 'What stays the same and what changes when you reflect the triangle into negative-coordinate regions?' Students write two sentences. Discuss: side lengths are preserved; coordinate values change sign but their squared differences do not.

Students work through End of Chapter Q4 (p.12): plot Z(5,−6), choose vertices I and N to form a right-angled triangle IZN, compute all three side lengths using the coordinate-difference method for the legs and the distance formula for the hypotenuse. Teacher checks construction choices and calculation steps.
Quick oral check: 'Which step in the distance formula derivation used the Baudhayana-Pythagoras theorem?' Two student responses, then close.

periods.teacher_notes: The distance formula is derived here from the Baudhayana-Pythagoras theorem applied to a right triangle built from coordinate differences — the horizontal and vertical shifts that the think-and-reflect asks students to reason about. A predictable slip is sign error when computing x2 − x1 for points in different quadrants: remind students that squaring makes the sign irrelevant, so they need only take the difference in any order and square it. End of Chapter Q16 (p.14) is a good self-study challenge for students who want to apply the formula to verify that a set of four plotted points form a square.

periods.activity_title: Applying the Distance Formula: Multi-Context Problem Solving
periods.visual_aids: Board sketch of the 800×600 pixel screen with two circles for End of Chapter Q15, showing the axes and centre coordinates

textbook_items_in_class.description: Given R(3,0), A(0,-2), M(-5,-2), P(-5,2) joined in order as quadrilateral RAMP, predict two perpendicular sides, one side parallel to an axis, and two points that are mirror images of each other in an axis; then plot and verify.

On an 800x600 pixel screen with origin at the bottom-left, given a radius-80 circle centred at A(100,150) and a radius-100 circle centred at B(250,230), determine whether any part of either circle lies outside the screen and whether the two circles intersect.
Plot A(2,1), B(-1,2), C(-2,-1), D(1,-2); determine whether ABCD is a square, explain why, and find its area.

time_bands.activity: Students work through End of Chapter Q3 (p.12): plotting R(3,0), A(0,−2), M(−5,−2), P(−5,2) on graph paper and using shared coordinates to predict and then verify two perpendicular sides, a side parallel to an axis, and which two vertices are mirror images in an axis. This consolidates both coordinate reading and the reflection idea from Section 1.4.

Students work through End of Chapter Q15 (p.14): on an 800×600 pixel screen with the origin at the bottom-left, checking whether each circle stays within the screen (comparing centre coordinate ± radius against the screen boundaries) and then computing the distance between A(100,150) and B(250,230) using the distance formula to compare with 80 + 100 = 180 and determine whether the circles intersect. Work individually, then pairs compare.

Students work through End of Chapter Q16 (p.14): plot A(2,1), B(−1,2), C(−2,−1), D(1,−2), compute all four side lengths and both diagonal lengths using the distance formula, argue that all four sides are equal and the diagonals are equal (so ABCD is a square), and find its area as the square of its side length. Teacher circulates, checking that students state a complete justification — equal sides alone do not suffice; equal diagonals distinguish a square from a rhombus.

Whole-class close: summarise the two uses of the distance formula seen across this unit and the previous one — straight-line distance between any two points, and the circle-intersection decision. Take two student-posed 'what-if' questions (for example, what would change in Q15 if the radius of A were 200?) to end on a generative note.

periods.teacher_notes: Having derived the distance formula in the preceding unit, students now apply it to problems that embed the computation inside a larger spatial question — screen boundaries, circle intersection, and square verification. A common error in End of Chapter Q16 is claiming that four equal sides alone prove the figure is a square; prompt students to also verify the diagonals are equal and to state why that additional check matters. End of Chapter Q5 (p.12) offers a reflective discussion item for a student who finishes early and wants to revisit how the coordinate system depends on negative numbers.

competency.competency_text: Specifying locations and describing spatial relationships using coordinate geometry.

questions.question_text: A grid-based location system was developed before Brahmagupta formalised zero and negative numbers. Which statement best explains why such an early grid could NOT describe the full four-quadrant coordinate plane?

options.label: A
options.text: Without a formal zero, the concept of distance between two points cannot be computed, making the grid useless for location.

options.label: B
options.text: Without a formal zero, the two axes cannot be defined as perpendicular number lines, so no axis can be drawn at all.

options.label: C
options.text: Without negative numbers, distances to the left of or below a reference point cannot be assigned a coordinate value, so only one quadrant of the plane can be addressed.

options.label: D
options.text: Without negative numbers, points on the positive x-axis and positive y-axis cannot be distinguished from each other.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Confuses the role of zero with the role of a perpendicular-lines construction — axes can be sketched geometrically; it is the number-line interpretation that needs zero and negative values to cover all four directions.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Conflates coordinate sign with axis identity — the x-axis and y-axis are distinguished by direction, not by the sign of coordinates placed on them.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Overstates the consequence: distance computations using only positive numbers are possible within one quadrant; the failure is locating points in the other three quadrants, not computing distances per se.

MCQ.inclusivity: A student who struggles with the abstract historical argument can be invited to draw a simple grid and shade only the region reachable with positive numbers, making the limitation concrete. A student who grasps this quickly can be asked to explain which specific quadrants become inaccessible and why each requires negative coordinates.

competency.competency_text: Specifying locations and describing spatial relationships using coordinate geometry.

questions.question_text: Two students each sketch the same 12 ft × 10 ft bedroom on a 1 cm = 1 ft grid. Student A places a pin for the door hinge at 3 cm from the left edge and 0 cm from the bottom edge. Student B places a pin for the same hinge at 3 cm from the right edge and 0 cm from the bottom edge. Both students claim their pin is correctly placed. (a) Explain why both students can be correct simultaneously. (b) Identify the single piece of information that is missing from the informal grid system that would make only one placement correct. (c) Explain how adding that missing structure produces an unambiguous description of the hinge's position.
look_for: Recognises that both placements are correct relative to each student's chosen reference corner, so neither is wrong given the informal system.
Identifies the missing element as a shared, fixed reference point (origin) with an agreed direction convention — not merely 'a ruler' or 'a scale'.

Explains that once a single corner is named as the origin with positive directions fixed, the hinge has exactly one pair of distances from the two walls passing through that corner, giving an unambiguous description.
Does not confuse the scale (1 cm = 1 ft) with the reference point — scale is already shared; what differs is the choice of corner.

ECR.inclusivity: A student who finds the written argument difficult can first mark both students' pins on a single grid sketch and point to the corner each student measured from, then narrate the explanation orally. A student who answers quickly can be asked to generalise: for an n × m room, how many different valid placements of the same pin exist in the informal system, and why?
ECR.lift_note: Rule 6 lift applied: the single implied LO for Section 1.2 reaches Understanding under a straightforward reading; it was lifted to ECR (Analysis) to satisfy the reasoning floor, as no other section in this chapter produces an Analysis or Evaluation item without the lift.

competency.competency_text: Specifying locations and describing spatial relationships using coordinate geometry.

questions.question_text: Point K lies in the third quadrant of the Cartesian plane. Point L lies on the negative y-axis. Which of the following correctly describes the signs of the coordinates of K and L?

options.label: A
options.text: K has a negative x-coordinate and a negative y-coordinate; L has a negative x-coordinate and y-coordinate 0.

options.label: B
options.text: K has a negative x-coordinate and a negative y-coordinate; L has x-coordinate 0 and a negative y-coordinate.

options.label: C
options.text: K has a negative x-coordinate and a positive y-coordinate; L has x-coordinate 0 and a negative y-coordinate.

options.label: D
options.text: K has a positive x-coordinate and a negative y-coordinate; L has x-coordinate 0 and a negative y-coordinate.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Confuses the third quadrant with the second quadrant (negative x, positive y); student has not correctly memorised or reasoned out the quadrant sign pattern.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Correctly identifies K but swaps the axes for L — places L on the negative x-axis instead of the negative y-axis, suggesting confusion between which coordinate is zero for a point on each axis.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Confuses the third quadrant with the fourth quadrant (positive x, negative y); another quadrant sign-pattern error.

MCQ.inclusivity: A student who is unsure about quadrant signs can be encouraged to draw the four-quadrant plane and label each quadrant's sign pattern before answering. A student who answers immediately can be asked to name the coordinates of a specific point on the negative y-axis and explain why its x-coordinate must be exactly zero.

competency.competency_text: Specifying locations and describing spatial relationships using coordinate geometry.

questions.question_text: A rectangular storage room has its back-left corner at the origin. The room extends 14 ft to the right along the x-axis and 9 ft upward along the y-axis. A shelving unit occupies the rectangular region with one corner at (4, 3) and the opposite corner at (10, 7). (a) Write down the coordinates of all four corners of the shelving unit. (b) The unit is shifted 2 ft to the right and 1 ft downward. Write the new coordinates of all four corners after the shift.
questions.method_one_line: Read the four corners of the rectangle from the two given opposite corners (sharing x and y values in pairs), then add (+2, −1) to each coordinate pair to apply the shift.

NUM.inclusivity: A student who finds part (b) difficult can be directed to plot the original four corners on graph paper and physically count 2 squares right and 1 square down to locate each new corner before writing coordinates. A student who completes both parts quickly can be asked to verify that the shifted unit still lies entirely within the 14 × 9 room and to write the inequality conditions that must hold for any corner (x, y) to remain inside the room.

competency.competency_text: Specifying locations and describing spatial relationships using coordinate geometry.

questions.question_text: Points P(−3, 4) and Q(5, −2) are given. (a) Construct the right triangle that the distance-formula derivation uses: name the coordinates of the third vertex R formed by drawing a horizontal from P and a vertical from Q (or vice versa), and state the lengths of the two legs PR and QR. (b) Apply the Baudhayana-Pythagoras theorem to find the length PQ. Leave your answer in surd form.
questions.method_one_line: Place the right-angle vertex at R(x2, y1) = (5, 4); the horizontal leg PR = |5 − (−3)| = 8 and the vertical leg QR = |4 − (−2)| = 6; then PQ = √(8² + 6²) = √100 = 10.

NUM.inclusivity: A student who struggles with negative coordinates in the leg calculation can be directed to compute |x2 − x1| and |y2 − y1| as absolute differences before squaring, emphasising that squaring a negative difference gives the same result. A student who finishes quickly can be asked to verify the answer by computing PQ a second way — using the formula directly with (x2 − x1)² = (5−(−3))² and (y2 − y1)² = (−2−4)² — and confirming both routes agree.

competency.competency_text: Specifying locations and describing spatial relationships using coordinate geometry.

questions.question_text: Four points are given: J(3, 1), K(1, 3), L(−3, −1), M(−1, −3). (a) Compute the four side lengths JK, KL, LM, MJ and both diagonal lengths JL and KM using the distance formula. Show all working. (b) Using your results, determine whether JKLM is a square. Justify your answer by stating which properties you have verified and which you have not.
look_for: Student notes that JK = LM = 2√2 and KL = MJ = 4√2, so opposite sides are equal but adjacent sides are not — the figure is a parallelogram (or rectangle), NOT a square.
Diagonal lengths: JL = √((−3−3)²+(−1−1)²) = √40 = 2√10; KM = √((−1−1)²+(−3−3)²) = √40 = 2√10. Equal diagonals confirm a rectangle.

Concludes clearly: JKLM is a rectangle (equal diagonals, opposite sides equal) but NOT a square because adjacent sides 2√2 and 4√2 are unequal. States which property (all sides equal) was not verified.
Does not claim equality of all four sides without computing — justification is calculation-based.

ECR.inclusivity: A student who finds tracking eight computations difficult can be directed to organise work in a table with columns: segment, Δx, Δy, (Δx)²+(Δy)², length. A student who concludes correctly can be challenged to identify the minimum set of distance computations that would suffice to rule out a square — is computing all four sides and both diagonals necessary, or can fewer values decide?
